𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates}: Privacy-Preserving and Immutable Audit Log for Sensitive Data Operations

Mohit Bhasi Thazhath, Jan Michalak, Thang Hoang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Virginia Tech, USA
{mohitbt, janmichalak, thanghoang}@vt.edu
Abstract

The audit log is a crucial component to monitor fine-grained operations over sensitive data (e.g., personal, health) for security inspection and assurance. Since such data operations can be highly sensitive, it is vital to ensure that the audit log achieves not only validity and immutability, but also confidentiality against active threats to standard data regulations (e.g., HIPAA) compliance. Despite its critical needs, state-of-the-art privacy-preserving audit log schemes (e.g., Ghostor (NSDI ’20), Calypso (VLDB ’19)) do not fully obtain a high level of privacy, integrity, and immutability simultaneously, in which certain information (e.g., user identities) is still leaked in the log.

In this paper, we propose 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates}, a new privacy-preserving and immutable audit log scheme. 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} permits data store, share, and access operations to be recorded in the audit log without leaking sensitive information (e.g., data identifier, user identity), while permitting the validity of data operations to be publicly verifiable. 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} makes use of blockchain techniques to achieve immutability and avoid a single point of failure, while cryptographic zero-knowledge proofs are harnessed for confidentiality and public verifiability. We analyze the security of our proposed technique and prove that it achieves non-malleability and indistinguishability. We fully implemented 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} and evaluated its performance on a real blockchain system (i.e., Hyperledger Fabric) deployed on a commodity platform (i.e., Amazon EC2). Experimental results demonstrated that 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} is highly scalable and achieves practical performance.

I Introduction

Remote data storage systems have become predominant in the past decade due to the growth of cloud computing. Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) have dedicated resources to store data, and have developed a suite of services to support it such as AWS S3, Azure Blobs, GCP Buckets. The widespread use of cloud data storage has made it easy to share/access remote data.

Given that CSPs generally maintain a vast amount of user data, many of which can be highly sensitive (e.g., personal, health), it is vital to maintain an audit log that records all the data operations (e.g., sharing, access activities) to support system integrity inspection and critical security assurances such as intrusion detection and problem analysis [1]. Many data audit log schemes have been proposed to record fine-grained operations (e.g., read, write, share) over sensitive data (e.g., Electronic Health Records (EHRs) [2, 3], supply chains [4, 5, 6, 7]) in a tamper-resistant and immutable manner.

Despite their merits, achieving the immutability and integrity of the audit log may not be sufficient to ensure security against active threats. This is because the audit log contains all data operations (i.e., metadata), which can reveal significant sensitive information. By analyzing the data log, the adversary can obtain the needed information without having to access the actual data [8]. Such metadata leakage has become notorious in related areas such as communication surveillance. A former NSA General Counsel stated, “Metadata absolutely tells you everything about somebody’s life” [9]. Due to the sensitivity of metadata, it is vital to ensure integrity and confidentiality of audit logs as indicated in standard data regulations such as The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) [10].

To enable both privacy and integrity, several privacy-preserving data audit log schemes have been proposed. Preliminary constructions permit data operations to be logged in a single server with privacy and integrity guarantees using cryptographic tools such as digital signatures and symmetric encryption [11, 12]. Despite their merits, such centralized approaches suffer from a single point of failure, in which the corrupted server can compromise the validity and confidentiality of the audit log. To address single point of failure, several decentralized privacy-preserving audit log approaches have been proposed using blockchain techniques [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. However, there are certain limitations to these techniques. For example, Droplet [17] offers confidentiality but not anonymity. Ghostor [18] records data sharing activities with anonymity, but the validity can only be verified privately by the data owner. This requires all the users to participate in the audit process to verify the validity of the data operations, thereby reducing the audit transparency. Calypso [19] achieves partial anonymity (i.e., leaks data owner identity) and private verifiability.

Research gaps. Given that existing data logging techniques lack a certain degree of anonymity, integrity, confidentiality, and transparency, our objective is to design a new privacy-preserving audit log scheme that can offer all desirable security properties for standard data regulations compliance.

Contribution. In this paper, we propose 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates}, a new privacy-preserving and immutable audit log scheme for sensitive data operations. 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} permits data operations (i.e., store, share, access) to be recorded in the audit log with validity, confidentiality, and public verifiability guarantees. 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} makes use of blockchain technologies (e.g., distributed ledger) to achieve immutability and validity, while confidentiality and public verifiability are achieved using advanced cryptographic techniques such as zero-knowledge proofs [20].

𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} achieves the following properties.

  • •

    Record Immutability: All the data operation records cannot be modified by anyone.

  • •

    Full Anonymity: The identity of the data and the user(s) remain hidden all the time. This security guarantee is stronger than existing works (e.g., [19, 17]).

  • •

    Publicly Verifiable Validity: Validity of the data operations (e.g., whether the share/access is performed by an authorized user) can be publicly verified by anyone. This improves audit transparency such that all the data users do not need to participate during the audit process.

  • •

    Temporal Access Control: Restricts the time for which the data can be accessed. This is useful when operating on highly sensitive data like EHRs.

Table Icompares 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} with state-of-the-art techniques. We rigorously analyze the security of our proposed technique and prove that it achieves standard security notions (non-malleability, indistinguishability). Finally, we implemented our technique and deployed it on a commodity platform (Amazon EC2) to evaluate its efficiency. Experimental results showed that 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} is highly scalable (§VII) and practical. Therefore, 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates}  can be used for sensitive data storage applications that require privacy-preserving audit log such as EHRs [13, 14] or supply chains [15, 16].

II-B Cryptographic Building blocks

Commitment Scheme. A commitment scheme is a tuple of Probabilistic Polynomial Time (PPT) algorithms (𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝒢,𝖢𝗈𝗆)(\mathsf{Com}.\mathcal{G},\mathsf{Com}) –

    𝗉𝗉←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}): Given a security parameter λ\lambda, it outputs public parameters 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp}.

  • •

    𝖼𝗆←𝖢𝗈𝗆r​(m,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r}(m,\mathsf{pp}): Given a message mm and a trapdoor rr, it outputs a commitment 𝖼𝗆\mathsf{cm}.

A commitment scheme is binding if for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that 𝗉𝗉←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}), (m0,m1,r0,r1)←𝒜⁡(𝗉𝗉)(m_{0},m_{1},r_{0},r_{1})\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(\mathsf{pp}), it holds that 𝖯𝗋[𝖢𝗈𝗆r0(m0,𝗉𝗉)=𝖢𝗈𝗆r1(m1,𝗉𝗉)∧m0≠m1]≤𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)\mathsf{Pr}\left[\mathsf{Com}_{r_{0}}(m_{0},\mathsf{pp})=\mathsf{Com}_{r_{1}}(m_{1},\mathsf{pp})\land m_{0}\neq m_{1}\right]\leq\mathsf{negl}(\lambda); hiding if for any PPT 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that (m0,m1)←𝒜(𝗉𝗉),b←$0,1,r←${0,1}λ,𝖼𝗆←𝖢𝗈𝗆rb(mb,𝗉𝗉),b′←𝒜(𝖼𝗆)(m_{0},m_{1})\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(\mathsf{pp}),b\xleftarrow{\$}{0,1},r\xleftarrow{\$}\{0,1\}^{\lambda},\mathsf{cm}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r_{b}}(m_{b},\mathsf{pp}),b^{\prime}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(\mathsf{cm}), it holds that |𝖯𝗋[b=b′]−12|≤𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)|\mathsf{Pr}[b=b^{\prime}]-\frac{1}{2}|\leq\mathsf{negl}(\lambda).

Merkle Tree. Merkle tree permits to commit to a set of values with the ability to reveal an element in the committed set later (proof of membership). Given m→=(m1,m2,m3,…,mn)\vec{m}=(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},\dotsc,m_{n}), it first initializes a binary tree TT with nn leaves and H⁡(mi)H(m_{i}) be the ii-th leaf node. TT is built bottom-up, where each non-leaf node tt of TT is computed by computing the hash of its child nodes t𝗅t_{\mathsf{l}} and t𝗋t_{\mathsf{r}}, i.e., t=H(t𝗅||t𝗋)t=H(t_{\mathsf{l}}||t_{\mathsf{r}}). The verifier recomputes 𝗋𝗍\mathsf{rt} using 𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁\mathsf{path} for membership verification.

Argument of Knowledge. An argument of knowledge for an NP relation ℛ\mathcal{R} is a protocol between a prover 𝒫\mathcal{P} and a verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V}, in which 𝒫\mathcal{P} convinces 𝒱\mathcal{V} that it knows a witness ww for some input in an NP language x∈ℒx\in\mathcal{L} such that (x,w)∈ℛ(x,w)\in\mathcal{R}. Formally speaking, a zero-knowledge argument of knowledge is a tuple of PPT algorithms 𝗓𝗄𝗉=(𝒢,𝒫,𝒱)\mathsf{zkp}=(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{V}) as follows.

  • •

    𝗉𝗉←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}): Given a security parameter λ\lambda, it outputs public parameters 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp}.

  • •

    π←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒫⁡(x,w,𝗉𝗉)\pi\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{P}(x,w,\mathsf{pp}): Given a statement xx and a witness ww, it generates a proof π\pi to show (x,w)∈ℛ(x,w)\in\mathcal{R}.

  • •

    {0,1}←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒱⁡(x,π,𝗉𝗉)\{0,1\}\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{V}(x,\pi,\mathsf{pp}): Given a statement xx and a proof π\pi, it outputs 11 if π\pi is valid and (x,w)∈ℛ(x,w)\in\mathcal{R}, else it outputs 0.

An argument of knowledge is complete if for any (x,w)∈ℛ(x,w)\in\mathcal{R}, 𝗉𝗉←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}), π←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒫⁡(x,w,𝗉𝗉)\pi\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{P}(x,w,\mathsf{pp}), it holds that 𝖯𝗋[𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒱(x,π,𝗉𝗉)=1]=1\mathsf{Pr}\left[\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{V}(x,\pi,\mathsf{pp})=1\right]=1; is sound iff for any PPT prover 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}, there exists a PPT extractor ℰ\mathcal{E}, when given the entire execution and randomness of 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}, ℰ\mathcal{E} can extract a witness ww such that 𝗉𝗉←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}), π∗←𝒫∗​(x,𝗉𝗉)\pi^{*}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}^{*}(x,\mathsf{pp}), w←ℰ𝒫∗​(x,π∗,𝗉𝗉)w\leftarrow\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{P}^{*}}(x,\pi^{*},\mathsf{pp}) and 𝖯𝗋[𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒱(x,π,𝗉𝗉)=1∧(x,w)∉ℛ]≤𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)\mathsf{Pr}\left[\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{V}(x,\pi,\mathsf{pp})=1\land(x,w)\notin\mathcal{R}\right]\leq\mathsf{negl}(\lambda); is zero-knowledge iff for any PPT verifier 𝒱∗\mathcal{V}^{*} there exists simulators (S1,S2)(S_{1},S_{2}) –

𝖯𝗋⁡[𝗉𝗉←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒢⁡(1λ)π←𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒫⁡(x,w,𝗉𝗉)𝗓𝗄𝗉.𝒱⁡(x,π,𝗉𝗉)=1]≈𝖯𝗋⁡[𝗉𝗉←S1​(1λ)π←S2​(x,𝗉𝗉)𝒱∗​(x,π,𝗉𝗉)=1]\mathsf{Pr}\left[\begin{array}[]{r}\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda})\\ \pi\leftarrow\mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{P}(x,w,\mathsf{pp})\\ \mathsf{zkp}.\mathcal{V}(x,\pi,\mathsf{pp})=1\end{array}\right]\approx\mathsf{Pr}\left[\begin{array}[]{r}\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow S_{1}(1^{\lambda})\\ \pi\leftarrow S_{2}(x,\mathsf{pp})\\ \mathcal{V}^{*}(x,\pi,\mathsf{pp})=1\end{array}\right]

III Models

System Model. In our system, there are three types of participants: (i) The data owner 𝒪\mathcal{O} who owns some data; (ii) The data user 𝒰\mathcal{U} who would like to access 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s data; (iii) The storage provider 𝒮\mathcal{S} that provides storage facilities to store 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s data remotely. Our system permits data storage, sharing, and access between these participants while, at the same time, recording all the data operations in a distributed audit log for auditability. A Privacy-preserving and Immutable Audit Log (PIAL) scheme consists of the following PPT algorithms –

  • •

    (ℒ,𝗉𝗉)←𝖨𝗇𝗂𝗍⁡(1λ,N)(\mathcal{L},\mathsf{pp})\leftarrow\mathsf{Init}(1^{\lambda},N): Given a security parameter λ\lambda, and the maximum number of supported operations NN, it outputs an initial distributed audit log ℒ\mathcal{L} and public parameters 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp}.

  • •

    (𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋)←𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Register}(1^{\lambda}): Given a security parameter λ\lambda, it outputs an address-key pair (𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}) as an identifier for the participant.

  • •

    (𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗍𝗋)←𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾⁡(D,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,𝗉𝗉CLOSE(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{str}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Store}(D,\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},\mathsf{pp}): Given data DD, 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, it outputs a store token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}} and a store record 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{str}}.

  • •

    (𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇)←𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,𝗉𝗉)(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}})\leftarrow\mathsf{AssignOwner}(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},\mathsf{pp}): Given 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, and 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}, it outputs an ownership token 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}, which permits 𝒪\mathcal{O} to share her data stored on 𝒮\mathcal{S} later, and create a record of ownership 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}.

  • •

    (𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗁𝗋)←𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾⁡(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰,𝗍𝗌,𝗉𝗉)(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{shr}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Share}(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}},\mathsf{ts},\mathsf{pp}): Given 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}, 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}, 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}}, a share expiry timestamp 𝗍𝗌>0\mathsf{ts}>0, it outputs a data share token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} that is only valid up to 𝗍𝗌\mathsf{ts}, and a record of share 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{shr}}.

  • •

    (𝗍𝗄𝖺𝖼𝖼,𝗍𝗑𝖺𝖼𝖼)←𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮.𝗉𝗉)(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{acc}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{acc}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Access}(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}.\mathsf{pp}): Given 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}}, 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, it outputs a data access token 𝗍𝗄𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{acc}} (if 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} is not expired) and a record of access 𝗍𝗑𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{acc}}.

  • •

    {0,1}←𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖫𝗈𝗀⁡(𝗍𝗑,ℒ,𝗉𝗉)\{0,1\}\leftarrow\mathsf{VerifyLog}(\mathsf{tx},\mathcal{L},\mathsf{pp}): Given a record 𝗍𝗑\mathsf{tx} and audit log ℒ\mathcal{L}, it outputs 11 if the record is valid else 00.

Threat and Security Models. We assume participants do not trust each other, i.e., they can behave maliciously toward the records created by other participants. The adversary is curious about the record content, e.g., who is the owner of a particular data, whom the data is shared with or accessed by, and what data is being shared or accessed. The adversary may also attempt to modify the record to compromise validity or to gain unauthorized access. We aim to achieve integrity and confidentiality properties for the audit log via record non-malleability and audit log indistinguishability as follows.

Definition 1 (Record Non-Malleability).

Let Π\Pi be a candidate PIAL scheme. Consider experiment NMGameΠ,𝒜​(λ)\texttt{NMGame}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda) between the adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the challenger 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} samples 𝗉𝗉←𝖨𝗇𝗂𝗍⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{Init}(1^{\lambda}) and sends 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp} to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then, 𝒞\mathcal{C} initializes a PIAL oracle 𝒪𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}} using 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp} with audit log ℒ\mathcal{L}. At each time step, 𝒜\mathcal{A} adaptively specifies a query q∈{𝖢𝗋𝖾𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖠𝖽𝖽𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗌q\in\{\mathsf{CreateAddress}, 𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Store}, 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{AssignOwner}, 𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Share}, 𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌}\mathsf{Access}\} to 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} forwards qq to 𝒪𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}, receives a response and forwards it to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} also provides the view of ℒ\mathcal{L} to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputs a record 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the set of records with the same type of 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} that 𝒪𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}} generates during the query phase.

If there exists a record 𝗍𝗑∈𝒯\mathsf{tx}\in\mathcal{T} created in response to a query, 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins and outputs 1 iff the following conditions hold – (i) m∗≠mm^{*}\neq m; (ii) 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖫𝗈𝗀⁡(𝗍𝗑∗,𝗉𝗉,ℒ′)=1\mathsf{VerifyLog}(\mathsf{tx}^{*},\mathsf{pp},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})=1, where ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} is the state of the audit log preceding 𝗍𝗑\mathsf{tx}; iii) if 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} is a record of ownership, 𝗌𝗇∗=𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}^{*}=\mathsf{sn}. Otherwise, it outputs 0.

Π\Pi is said to achieve record non-malleability if 𝖯𝗋[NMGameΠ,𝒜(λ)=1]≤𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)\mathsf{Pr}[{\texttt{NMGame}}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)=1]\leq\mathsf{negl}(\lambda).

Definition 2 (Audit Log Indistinguishability).

Let Π\Pi be a candidate PIAL scheme. Consider experiment IndGameΠ,𝒜​(λ)\texttt{IndGame}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda) between 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} first samples a random bit b←${0,1}b\xleftarrow{\$}\{0,1\}, 𝗉𝗉←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}) and initializes two PIAL oracles 𝒪0𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{0} and 𝒪1𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{1}, where each oracle 𝒪i𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{i} has a separate audit log ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} as well as internal variables. At each time step, 𝒜\mathcal{A} adaptively specifies two queries Q,Q′Q,Q^{\prime} of the same type (one of 𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾,𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋,𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾,𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Store},\mathsf{AssignOwner},\mathsf{Share},\mathsf{Access}). 𝒞\mathcal{C} forwards QQ to 𝒪0𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{0}, Q′Q^{\prime} to 𝒪1𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{1} and receives the corresponding answers R0,R1R_{0},R_{1}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} forwards (Rb,R1−b)(R_{b},R_{1-b}) to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} also provides to 𝒜\mathcal{A} two ledgers ℒ𝗅𝖾𝖿𝗍=ℒb\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{left}}=\mathcal{L}_{b}, ℒ𝗋𝗂𝗀𝗁𝗍=ℒ1−b\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{right}}=\mathcal{L}_{1-b}, where ℒb\mathcal{L}_{b} is the current audit log in 𝒪b𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{b}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputs a bit b′∈{0,1}b^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins if b′=bb^{\prime}=b and outputs 11 else 0.

Π\Pi is said to achieve audit log indistinguishability if 𝖯𝗋[IndGameΠ,𝒜(λ)=1]≤12+𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)\mathsf{Pr}[{\texttt{IndGame}}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)=1]\leq\frac{1}{2}+\mathsf{negl}(\lambda).

IV Our Proposed Method

IV-A Overview

𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} supports three data operations – store, share, and access, wherein each operation is recorded in a distributed audit log (i.e., blockchain).

The high-level workflow (ref. Figure 1) is as follows, given a data dd to be stored on 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒪\mathcal{O} creates “store” record (1) and a token for 𝒮\mathcal{S} containing the message digest of dd, while sending dd off-chain to 𝒮\mathcal{S} for storage. The nodes in the blockchain then verify the validity of the store record (2) before recording it to the audit log. 𝒮\mathcal{S} then creates an “ownership” record that certifies the ownership of 𝒪\mathcal{O} on the data and provides a token (3) that permits 𝒪\mathcal{O} to share her data with 𝒰\mathcal{U} later. To share the data, 𝒪\mathcal{O} creates a “share” record (4) demonstrating her ownership, which is then verified by the blockchain before being appended to the audit log (5). The user then accesses this record to obtain a share token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} (6) indicating the authorization to access the shared data stored on 𝒮\mathcal{S} for a limited period of time. To access the shared data, the user creates an “access” record (7) demonstrating the access is authorized by the owner, and an access token for 𝒮\mathcal{S} to serve the request. Finally, the record (8) is verified by the blockchain and included in the audit log. If it is valid, 𝒮\mathcal{S} sends data (9) to the requested user 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

To ensure all the data operations are confidential (e.g., hides participant identity or which data is being shared/accessed), while permitting public verification, we harness cryptographic commitment, encryption, and zero-knowledge techniques inspired by Zerocash [21].

IV-B Detailed Construction

IV-B1 Initialization

The initialization generates public parameters for NP-statements to be proven/verified in zero-knowledge. We initialize four empty Merkle trees with roots (𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗋𝗍𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝗋𝗍𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{acc}}), each containing commitments of the corresponding data operation being performed. We assume 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} permits up to NN number of operations per type.

Figure 2presents the initialization in detail. Since 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} operates on a distributed audit log, each participant needs an address keypair for communication and logging their data operations by using 𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Register}.

Since (𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}) is never revealed, each participant is free to re-use a single address for all operations.

IV-B2 Data Store Protocol

Figure 3 presents our data store protocol. Given data DD, 𝒪\mathcal{O} first creates a commitment formed by the hash of the data H⁡(D)H(D), 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}} and a random value ρ\rho as 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋←𝖢𝗈𝗆r​(H⁡(D)​‖𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮‖​ρ,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r}(H(D)||\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}||\rho,\mathsf{pp}) (Figure 3, line 3). 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}} is needed in 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} to tie store request of DD with 𝒮\mathcal{S}. On the other hand, the random ρ\rho is used to ensure that the request can only be handled once (see §IV-B3).

𝒪\mathcal{O} generates a one-time unique signing key pair (𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀,𝗌𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{sig}}) to sign their store request (Figure 3, line 4). This ensures unlinkability between multiple requests from 𝒪\mathcal{O}. To achieve non-repudiation and prevent malleability attacks, such keys must be tied with 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}. Thus, 𝒪\mathcal{O} creates a MAC tag hh of the signing key 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}} under their address private key 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}} as h←𝖯𝖱𝖥⁡(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,h𝗌𝗂𝗀)h\leftarrow\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},h_{\mathsf{sig}}), where h𝗌𝗂𝗀←H⁡(𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀)h_{\mathsf{sig}}\leftarrow H(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}) (Figure 3, line 5). For creating a store record, 𝒪\mathcal{O} needs to show that the components of (𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋,h)(\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}},h) have been formed correctly under their secrets (𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,r,ρ,v,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,h𝗌𝗂𝗀)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},r,\rho,v,\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},h_{\mathsf{sig}}).

NP-statements for Data Store. Given a store instance x=(𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋,h)x=(\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}},h), the witness w=(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,r,ρ,v,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,h𝗌𝗂𝗀)w=(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},r,\rho,v,\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},h_{\mathsf{sig}}) is a valid witness for xx if the following holds –

  • •

    The commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} is well-formed, i.e., 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋=𝖢𝗈𝗆r​(H⁡(D)​‖𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮‖​ρ,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}}=\mathsf{Com}_{r}(H(D)||\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}||\rho,\mathsf{pp}).

  • •

    The address secret key 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}} ties h𝗌𝗂𝗀h_{\mathsf{sig}} to hh, i.e., h=𝖯𝖱𝖥(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪||h𝗌𝗂𝗀)h=\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}||h_{\mathsf{sig}}).

𝒪\mathcal{O} then creates a store token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋←ℰ.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,r​||ρ|​|v||​𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋)\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}\leftarrow\mathcal{E}.\mathsf{Enc}(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},r||\rho||v||\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}}) containing the openings of the commitment and encrypts it under 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s public key (Figure 3, line 9). This token will be used by 𝒮\mathcal{S} to respond to 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s request appropriately. 𝒪\mathcal{O} forms a store record 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{str}}, which contains the commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}}, the MAC tag hh, the encrypted token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}, proof π𝗌𝗍𝗋\pi_{\mathsf{str}}, and the signature verification key 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. We store the token in the record to help with auditing. During an audit, 𝒪\mathcal{O} simply uses their secret key to decrypt the token and verify record contents. Finally, 𝒪\mathcal{O} signs the record with 𝗌𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{sig}}, and broadcasts it to the distributed audit log while sending the data DD to 𝒮\mathcal{S}. 𝒮\mathcal{S} checks if the decrypted store token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}} is consistent with the commitment and the record is valid (i.e., valid signature and valid proof). If so, 𝒮\mathcal{S} stores DD in an appropriate location and creates a record to give the ownership to 𝒪\mathcal{O}.

IV-B3 Assign Ownership Protocol

𝒮\mathcal{S} performs an assign ownership operation on receiving a 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}. 𝒮\mathcal{S} decrypts 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}} to identify which data needs to be assigned. A serial number 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn} is generated using the seed ρ\rho (Figure 3, line 14) in the store record. 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn} uses a collision-resistant 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} function to ensure that only one assignment is created for the corresponding store operation. Without this, 𝒮\mathcal{S} can use a single 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}} to maliciously perform assign operations to multiple data owners. Subsequently, 𝒮\mathcal{S} generates a commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇←𝖢𝗈𝗆r′(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝖽𝗋𝒪||v′,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r^{\prime}}(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{addr}}^{\mathcal{O}}||v^{\prime},\mathsf{pp}) (Figure 3, line 15) to represent ownership assignment. To successfully create an assign record, 𝒮\mathcal{S} generates a proof of ownership π𝗈𝗐𝗇\pi_{\mathsf{own}} (Figure 3, line 21). Verification of the proof shows that 𝒮\mathcal{S} received a store request for the corresponding data. The proof is generated by the following NP statements –

NP-statements for Data Owner Assignment. Given an assign owner instance x=(𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗌𝗇,𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇,h)x=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{sn},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}},h), the witness w=(𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,ρ,r,v,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,r′,v′,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,h𝗌𝗂𝗀)w=(\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},\rho,r,v,\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},r^{\prime},v^{\prime},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},h_{\mathsf{sig}}) is a valid witness for xx if the following holds –

  • •

    Commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} appears in the Merkle tree 𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}, i.e., 𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋=H(…(H(H(𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋)||𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗌𝗍𝗋d)||𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗌𝗍𝗋d−1)||…||𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗌𝗍𝗋1))\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}=H(\dots(H(H(\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}})||\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{str}}^{d})||\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{str}}^{d-1})||\dots||\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{str}}^{1})) where dd is the height of the Merkle tree and 𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗌𝗍𝗋i\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{str}}^{i} represents the sibling node at height ii.

  • •

    Commitments 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} and 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}} are well-formed.

  • •

    Serial number 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn} is computed correctly, i.e., 𝗌𝗇=𝖯𝖱𝖥(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮||ρ)\mathsf{sn}=\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}||\rho)

  • •

    Values committed to 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} and 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}} are the same.

  • •

    The address secret key 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}} ties h𝗌𝗂𝗀h_{\mathsf{sig}} to hh.

We utilize Merkle trees to prove set membership i.e, the statement to prove 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} appears in 𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}. The tree is stored locally by the blockchain nodes and only the root is added to the record. This is because we want to capture the state of the tree when the particular record was created. 𝒮\mathcal{S} then creates an encrypted ownership token 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}} (Figure 3, line 22). Finally, 𝒮\mathcal{S} signs record 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}, using a one-time signing key, and appends it to the distributed audit log. 𝒮\mathcal{S} also sends 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}} to 𝒪\mathcal{O}.

IV-B4 Sharing Protocol

Given an ownership token 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}, a share expiry timestamp 𝗍𝗌\mathsf{ts}, 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}} and 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}} a share operation generates a share token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} to 𝒰\mathcal{U} and a record 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{shr}}. A commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}} is created to 𝒰\mathcal{U}, share expiry timestamp and the hash of the data being shared (Figure 4, line 1). 𝒪\mathcal{O} generates a valid proof π𝗌𝗁𝗋\pi_{\mathsf{shr}} (Figure 4, line 7) by proving the following NP statements –

NP-statements for Data Sharing. Given a share instance x=(𝗋𝗍𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋,h)x=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}},h), the witness w=(𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,r,v,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰,r′,v′,h𝗌𝗂𝗀,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪)w=(\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},r,v,\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}},r^{\prime},v^{\prime},h_{\mathsf{sig}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}) is a valid witness for xx if the following holds –

  • •

    Commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}} appears in the Merkle tree 𝗋𝗍𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{own}}.

  • •

    Commitments 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}} and 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}} are well-formed.

  • •

    Values committed to 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}} and 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}} are the same.

  • •

    The expiration timestamp committed to 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}} is valid, i.e., 𝗍𝗌≥0\mathsf{ts}\geq 0.

  • •

    The address secret key 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}} ties h𝗌𝗂𝗀h_{\mathsf{sig}} to hh.

Verification of this proof means that 𝒪\mathcal{O} owns the corresponding data being shared and is sharing it for a valid period of time. Once the proof is generated, all the generated data is bundled into a record 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{shr}} and signed using 𝗌𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{sig}} (Figure 4, line 10). The record is added to the distributed audit log for verification and the token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} is sent to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Note that 𝒪\mathcal{O} can share their data multiple times because they can re-use their token 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}} more than once.

IV-B5 Access Protocol

𝒰\mathcal{U} uses 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} obtained from 𝒪\mathcal{O} to perform an access operation. A commitment representing an access 𝖼𝗆𝖺𝖼𝖼←𝖢𝗈𝗆r′(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮||v′,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{acc}}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r^{\prime}}(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}||v^{\prime},\mathsf{pp}) is generated using 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s public key and the hash of the data that needs to be accessed (Figure 4, line 13). 𝒰\mathcal{U} then creates a proof π𝖺𝖼𝖼\pi_{\mathsf{acc}} by proving the following –

NP-statements for Data Access. Given an access instance x=(𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝖼𝗆𝖺𝖼𝖼,h)x=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{acc}},h), the witness w=(𝗉𝖺𝗍𝗁𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰,r,v,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,r′,v′,𝗍𝗌,𝖼𝗎𝗋𝗋,h𝗌𝗂𝗀,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰)w=(\mathsf{path}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}},r,v,\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},r^{\prime},v^{\prime},\mathsf{ts},\mathsf{curr},h_{\mathsf{sig}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}}) is a valid witness for xx if the following holds –

  • •

    Commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}} appears in Merkle tree 𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{shr}}.

  • •

    Commitments 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}} and 𝖼𝗆𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{acc}} are well-formed.

  • •

    Values committed to 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}} and 𝖼𝗆𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{acc}} are the same.

  • •

    The timestamp committed to 𝖼𝗆𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{acc}} is not expired, i.e., 0<𝖼𝗎𝗋𝗋<𝗍𝗌0<\mathsf{curr}<\mathsf{ts} where 𝖼𝗎𝗋𝗋\mathsf{curr} is the current timestamp.

  • •

    The address secret key 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}} ties h𝗌𝗂𝗀h_{\mathsf{sig}} to hh.

A valid proof for the above statements can only be generated if 𝒰\mathcal{U} was given the share token by 𝒪\mathcal{O} and the share expiry timestamp is not expired. We note that 𝒰\mathcal{U} can access the data as many times as they wish within the given time period after which they will not be able to generate a valid π𝖺𝖼𝖼\pi_{\mathsf{acc}}. Finally, 𝒰\mathcal{U} creates an access record (Figure 4, line 23) and appends it to the distributed audit log. 𝒰\mathcal{U} also sends the access token to the 𝒮\mathcal{S} to obtain the data shared with them. 𝒮\mathcal{S} sends the data only if the record (i.e 𝗍𝗑𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{acc}}) corresponding to 𝗍𝗄𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{acc}} has been validated by the distributed audit log.

IV-B6 Record Verification

The 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽\mathsf{VerifyRecord} protocol (see Figure 5) runs on the distributed audit log nodes to verify the zero-knowledge proof and the signature included in the record. If either of the verification procedures fails, the record is discarded. If the record verification succeeds, the audit log nodes update their local copies of the corresponding commitment tree and appends the record to the audit log.

V Security Analysis

Theorem 1.

𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} satisfies record non-malleability by Definition 1.

Proof (sketch).

Let Q𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋={1λ,1λ,…}Q_{\mathsf{Register}}=\{1^{\lambda},1^{\lambda},\dotsc\} be the queries by 𝒜\mathcal{A} to 𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Register} and R𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋={(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,1,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,1),(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,2,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,2),…}R_{\mathsf{Register}}=\{(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},1},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},1}),(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},2},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},2}),\dotsc\} be 𝒞\mathcal{C}’s response.

Without loss of generality, let Q𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋={(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋1,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,1,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,1,𝗉𝗉),(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋2,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,2,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,2,𝗉𝗉),,…}Q_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}}=\{(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}^{1},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},1},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O},1},\mathsf{pp}),(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}^{2},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},2},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O},2},\mathsf{pp}),,\dotsc\} be the queries created by 𝒜\mathcal{A} and R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋={(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇1,𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇1),(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇2,𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇2),…}R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}}=\{(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{1},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{1}),(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{2},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{2}),\dotsc\} be the response by 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins the experiment NMGame when it outputs a record 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∗\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*} such that (i) m∗≠mm^{*}\neq m, where mm is the message in some 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∈R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}\in R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}}; (ii) 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖫𝗈𝗀⁡(𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,ℒ′,𝗉𝗉)=1\mathsf{VerifyLog}(\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},\mathcal{L}^{\prime},\mathsf{pp})=1, where ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} is the state of the audit log preceding 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}; (iii) 𝗌𝗇∗=𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}^{*}=\mathsf{sn} iff 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} is an ownership record.

Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins by creating a record 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∗=(𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋∗,𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗,σ∗,𝗌𝗇∗,𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,h∗,π𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇∗)\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}^{*},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*},\sigma^{*},\mathsf{sn}^{*},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},h^{*},\pi_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}) with proof instance x∗=(𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋∗,𝗌𝗇∗,𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,h∗)x^{*}=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}^{*},\mathsf{sn}^{*},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},h^{*}) and m∗=x∗||h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗|​|π𝗈𝗐𝗇∗||𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇∗m^{*}=x^{*}||h_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}||\pi_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}||\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}. We consider the following events.

E1:E_{1}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, and there exists 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∈R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}\in R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}} such that 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}=\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. To win, 𝒜\mathcal{A} produces σ∗\sigma^{*} such that Σ.𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗,m∗,σ∗)=1\Sigma.\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*},m^{*},\sigma^{*})=1, m∗≠mm^{*}\neq m and 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}=\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. However, due to the SUF-CMA property of the signature scheme [22], this happens with negligible probability.

E2:E_{2}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, E1E_{1} does not occur, and there exists 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∈R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}\in R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}} such that h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=h𝗌𝗂𝗀h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}=h_{\mathsf{sig}}. When 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, it crafts a h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=h𝗌𝗂𝗀h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}=h_{\mathsf{sig}} when 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗≠𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}\neq\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. However, the hash function [23] is collision-resistant, a contradiction.

E3:E_{3}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, (E1,E2)(E_{1},E_{2}) do not occur and h∗=𝖯𝖱𝖥(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗||h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗)h^{*}=\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}||h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}) for some 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗∈R𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}\in R_{\mathsf{Register}}. Due to the one-wayness property of 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} (used to generate 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}), 𝒜\mathcal{A} will not be able to deduce 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}} and generates h∗h^{*} with a random key. However, due to indistinguishability property of 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} (used to generate h∗h^{*}), 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins negligbly.

E4:E_{4}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, (E1,E2,E3)(E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}) do not occur, 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} is an ownership record and h∗≠𝖯𝖱𝖥(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗||h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗)h^{*}\neq\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}||h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}) for all 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗∈R𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}\in R_{\mathsf{Register}}. If 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, it outputs a modified record such that 𝗌𝗇∗=𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}^{*}=\mathsf{sn}. However, since in E4E_{4} 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗≠𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}\neq\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, it means that to generate 𝗌𝗇∗\mathsf{sn}^{*}, 𝒜\mathcal{A} found a collision in the 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} needed to generate 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn} which occurs with negligible probability due to the collision-resistant property of the 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} function used to generate 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}. ∎

Theorem 2.

𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} satisfies audit log indistinguishability by Definition 2

Proof (sketch).

𝒞\mathcal{C} creates a simulation IndGameS\texttt{IndGame}_{S} that can answer the queries (Q,Q′Q,Q^{\prime}) independent to the selected bit bb as follows. 𝒞\mathcal{C} modifies the commitment 𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗍𝗋∗←𝖢𝗈𝗆r​(k,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{str}}^{*}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r}(k,\mathsf{pp}) by using random inputs k,rk,r. To answer 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{AssignOwner} queries, 𝒞\mathcal{C} modifies 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{AssignOwner} to create 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn} and hh randomly. 𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}} is computed like in 𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Store}. 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇∗←ℰ.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(e,p)\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}\leftarrow\mathcal{E}.\mathsf{Enc}(e,p) is generated using a random plaintext pp and key ee. Proof π𝗈𝗐𝗇∗←S⁡(x,𝗉𝗉)\pi_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}\leftarrow S(x,\mathsf{pp}) is computed using a simulator. To answer 𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Share} or 𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Access} queries, 𝒞\mathcal{C} computes hh, commitments (𝖼𝗆𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{shr}}/𝖼𝗆𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{acc}}), tokens (𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}}/𝗍𝗄𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{acc}}), proofs (π𝗌𝗁𝗋\pi_{\mathsf{shr}}/π𝖺𝖼𝖼\pi_{\mathsf{acc}}) by following modifications in 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{AssignOwner}.

We prove this by constructing a sequence of hybrid games and show that they are indistinguishable as follows. Let G0G_{0} be the original protocol IndGameΠ\texttt{IndGame}_{\Pi}. We define G1G_{1} as similar to G0G_{0}, except that 𝒞\mathcal{C} modifies the commitment in the response to use a 𝖼𝗆∗←𝖢𝗈𝗆r​(k,𝗉𝗉)\mathsf{cm}^{*}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}_{r}(k,\mathsf{pp}) by using random inputs k,rk,r. We have that G1≈cG0G_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{0} due to the hiding property of the commitment scheme.We define G2G_{2} as similar to G1G_{1}, except that the token in the response is replaced with 𝗍𝗄∗←ℰ.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(e,p)\mathsf{tk}^{*}\leftarrow\mathcal{E}.\mathsf{Enc}(e,p) where ee is a random public key and pp is a random plaintext. We argue that G2≈cG1G_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{1} due to the IND-CCA and IK-CCA properties of the encryption scheme [24]. We define G3G_{3} as similar to G2G_{2}, except that all 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} generated values (i.e, h,𝗌𝗇h,\mathsf{sn}) in the response are replaced with values generated using a random function. We say that G3≈cG2G_{3}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{2} due to the indistinguishability between 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} and random number function. Finally, we define G4G_{4} as similar to G3G_{3}, except that the zero-knowledge proof in the response is replaced by a simulated proof π∗←S⁡(x,𝗉𝗉)\pi^{*}\leftarrow S(x,\mathsf{pp}). We have that G4≈cG3G_{4}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{3} due to the zero-knowledge property of the proof system.

We can see that G4G_{4} is the simulation IndGameS\texttt{IndGame}_{S}. Therefore, IndGameΠ=G0≈cG1≈cG2≈cG3≈cG4=IndGameS\texttt{IndGame}_{\Pi}=G_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{3}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\approx}}G_{4}=\texttt{IndGame}_{S}. Since IndGameS\texttt{IndGame}_{S} can simulate the response to QQ and Q′Q^{\prime} independent of bit bb, 𝒜\mathcal{A} can win IndGameΠ\texttt{IndGame}_{\Pi} game with negligible probability. ∎

VI Implementation

We implemented 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} in Rust with 3,100 lines of code. We used Hyperledger Fabric [25] to set up the audit log as the distributed ledger. Each data operation was implemented as Hyperledger chaincode (equivalent to smart contracts) in Go. For the signature scheme, we implemented Schnorr signature scheme [22]. For the asymmetric encryption, we implemented ECIES with AES-GCM as the underlying symmetric encryption scheme [24]. For the commitment scheme, we used Pedersen commitment [26]. We implemented the Merkle trees with Poseidon hash function as it can efficiently compute hashes of two elements at once [27]. We implemented MiMC as the primary hash function as well as PRF due to its low multiplicative complexity [23]. Finally, our implementation made use of Bulletproofs [20] as the back-end zero-knowledge proof due to its small proof size and transparent setup.

We prove/verify statements in zero-knowledge for each data operation as follows –

Store. We implemented a circuit with one Pedersen commitment opening gadget 𝖯𝖾𝖽𝖦\mathsf{PedG} (based on [28]) to show knowledge of openings of a commitment and one hash pre-image gadget 𝖧𝗌𝗁𝖦\mathsf{HshG} (based on [23]) to show knowledge of a pre-image of a MiMC hash.

Assign. We implemented a circuit with one 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝖦\mathsf{MemG}, two 𝖯𝖾𝖽𝖦\mathsf{PedG}, and two 𝖧𝗌𝗁𝖦\mathsf{HshG}. Here, 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝖦\mathsf{MemG} is a Merkle tree based proof of membership gadget.

Share. We implemented a circuit with one range gadget 𝖱𝗀𝖾𝖦\mathsf{RgeG}, one 𝖧𝗌𝗁𝖦\mathsf{HshG}, one 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝖦\mathsf{MemG}, and two 𝖯𝖾𝖽𝖦\mathsf{PedG} gadgets. 𝖱𝗀𝖾𝖦\mathsf{RgeG} (based on [20]) is used to show knowledge that a value (𝗍𝗌\mathsf{ts} in our case) is within a given range.

Access. We implemented a circuit with 𝖱𝗀𝖾𝖦\mathsf{RgeG}, one 𝖧𝗌𝗁𝖦\mathsf{HshG}, one 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝖦\mathsf{MemG}, and two 𝖯𝖾𝖽𝖦\mathsf{PedG} gadgets.

VII Experimental Evaluation

VII-A Configuration

Hardware. We used 50 AWS EC2 t3.medium instances to deploy a Hyperledger Fabric blockchain network. Each instance had 4GB vRAM with a 2-core 3.1 GHz CPU (Intel Xeon) and network bandwidth of 4.3 Gbps. Nodes were deployed in the us-east-1 region.

Parameter Setting. We used standard parameters to achieve 128-bit security. We used standard Poseidon Hash parameters for the Merkle tree including width t=6t=6, full rounds RF=8R_{F}=8 and partial rounds Rp=130R_{p}=130 [27]. We used MiMC hash function with rate 512512 and capacity 513513. We implemented the Schnorr signature scheme to produce a 512-bit signature. For the ECIES encryption scheme, our implementation used a 256-bit public and secret key. We used Ed25519 curve of order 2255−192^{255}-19 for zero-knowledge proofs based on Bulletproofs, ECIES, and Schnorr. For Hyperledger Fabric, we set block size as 10 and the number of transaction confirmations as 1.

VII-B Micro-Benchmark

Table IIpresents the processing overhead in terms of circuit complexity, processing latency, and memory usage as well as the bandwidth overhead of each operation.

Circuit Complexity. Recording store operations incur the least circuit complexity, compared with other operations such as assign, share, and access. This is because performing a store operation only invokes one 𝖯𝖾𝖽𝖦\mathsf{PedG} and one 𝖧𝗌𝗁𝖦\mathsf{HshG}, while other operations invokes 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝖦\mathsf{MemG} along with other gadgets. The constraint system of 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝖦\mathsf{MemG} is complicated and requires proving and verifying (in zero-knowledge) d=64d=64 Poseidon hash pre-images, each of which incurs 3×t×RF+3×Rp=5343\times t\times R_{F}+3\times R_{p}=534 number of multiplication constraints [27]. Assign operation incurs a little higher circuit complexity than share and access because of an extra 𝖧𝗌𝗁𝖦\mathsf{HshG} used for 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}. Share has one constraint over access as it requires an additional constraint to calculate difference between the current timestamp, 𝖼𝗎𝗋𝗋\mathsf{curr} and the share expiry timestamp, 𝗍𝗌\mathsf{ts} (see §IV-B5).

Processing Latency. The processing latency depends on circuit complexity, especially the number of multiplication gates (|M||M|). Store operation incurs a small latency compared with other operations because it does not require checking set membership, which attributes to large circuit complexity. We include the Common Reference String (CRS) loading delay that is needed for the backend zero-knowledge proof (i.e., Bulletproofs), which takes around 1.51.5 seconds (s) in total. Without CRS, the proving and verification time for store operation is 0.35 s and 85 milliseconds (ms), respectively, which are about 60 times lesser than assign, share, and access. This matches their difference in |M|\lvert M\rvert.

Memory Usage. The memory usage also depends on the circuit complexity to prove each data operation. The CRS component takes approximately 3232 MB. Proving incurs more memory usage than verification, due to the space needed to store the witness.

Bandwidth. Since Bulletproof incurs a polylogarithmic proof size, the bandwidth overhead for each data operation is small. The proof size produced by Bulletproofs is 2​⌈log2⁡(|M|)⌉+132\lceil\log_{2}(|M|)\rceil+13 group elements. For store, |M|=644|M|=644 so its proof contains 2​⌈log2⁡(644)⌉+13=332\lceil\log_{2}(644)\rceil+13=33 group elements, which results in a total of 32⋅33=1,05632\cdot 33=1,056 bytes (B). For assign, share, and access operations, |M|≈37,000|M|\approx 37,000 and, their proof size is 1,440 B.

VII-C Macro-Benchmark

We benchmark the performance of 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} using Hyperledger Fabric. We vary the number of concurrent records kk and blockchain nodes nn to evaluate the scalability of our proposed technique.

Overall latency. Figure 6 presents the latency to verify a data operation with varying kk and nn. When k=25k=25 and n=10n=10, it takes around 17 s to verify a record of assign, share, and access operations (see 6(a)). We see that the verification delay reduces when increasing nn. In particular, it reduces to around 11 s for n=20n=20, and 9 s for n=30n=30, after which, we observe no further improvement. This is because, when n=30n=30, every node only verifies one operation at a time. Notice that verifying an assign record should only take 8.5 s (from micro-benchmark), rather than 9 s as shown in Figure 6 (when n≥kn\geq k). This is due to the delay caused by Hyperledger Fabric implementation of about 0.5 s. The same trend is observed for store operation, where the latency is 4.13 s when n=10n=10 and reduces to 2.51 s and 2 s when n=20n=20 and n=30n=30, respectively.

6(b)and 6(c) shows the impact on verification latency when increasing kk. We observe that when doubling kk, the latency does not doubly increase but increases around 2 - 1.5 times. This is due to the implementation of Hyperledger Fabric, which attempts to exploit all the CPU resources (2 cores in our setting) to verify all records submitted to it. The speedup is not observed when n=10n=10 because the load per node is 5 (when k=50k=50) or 7.5 (when k=75k=75). The 5/7.5 verifications happen at the same time across 2 CPU cores. This requires the CPUs to constantly switch between tasks which incurs a large delay.

Figure 8presents end-to-end processing latency when n=30n=30 with varying kk. It captures proving time (including overhead to load CRS), record creation time, verification time, and consensus delays.

Memory Usage. Figure 7 presents distribution of memory used by nodes with varying kk and nn. In 7(a), when k=25k=25 and n=10n=10, the median memory used to verify a store/assign/share/access operation is about 171/279/271/271 MB, respectively. Similar to latency, we see that the memory used by nodes to verify records of data operations reduces when increasing nn. For example, the inter-quartile range of memory usage when n=20n=20 and k=25k=25 for a store operation is 130-151 MB with a median of 132 MB. This is because the majority of the nodes verify one store operation and some handle two as seen by the maximum value of 172 MB. When n=50n=50 and k=25k=25, half the nodes verify one store operation and the other half are idle, therefore, we observe an inter-quartile range of 92-131 MB with a median of 110 MB. The lower quartile of 92 MB shows the memory needed to run Hyperledger Fabric. The upper quartile of 131 MB shows the memory needed to verify one store operation.

As seen in 7(b) and 7(c), increasing kk increases the memory usage by the blockchain nodes as observed by the tighter inter-quartile range. However, the maximum memory used, regardless of kk, is about 174/282/272/271 MB for store/assign/share/access operations . This is equivalent to verifying two operations at a time since every node only has two CPUs.

VII-D Comparison with prior works

We conservatively compare the performance of our scheme with some prior works related to our setting including Ghostor [18] and Calypso [19]. Table III presents the end-to-end delays incurred to perform one data operation of our scheme and prior works. Ghostor incurs the least delay of an average of 7 seconds mostly due to the asymmetric encryption and Tor anonymous communication. Calypso incurs the second highest delay of around 16 seconds for each operation mainly as it relies on verifiable secret sharing. A data operation in 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates}~ takes about 33 seconds mostly due to zero-knowledge proof of membership, which accounts for about 80% of the delay. However, despite being slower than prior works, we note that our scheme permits public verifiability for data operations thereby, making the audit process transparent. In prior works, the log must be validated by a trusted auditor and requires all the data operators to participate in the audit process.

VIII Related Work

Centralized Audit Log. Traditional data sharing/access schemes record data operations directly on the server that stores the data [29, 30]. Such records are needed for audit purposes, where a third-party auditor determines whether any unauthorized accesses have been made in the system [1, 31]. However, with the introduction of regulations like HIPAA a secure logging mechanism [10] is needed. Secure logging primitives [11, 32] rely on a trusted author whose signature is considered the root of trust for integrity or requires analyzing the entirety of the audit log to detect tampering due to the privacy-preserving nature of the records. Alternatively, prior works [33, 12] use secure hardware to achieve immutable and privacy-preserving records. Since the audit log is maintained by the centralized server, it is vulnerable to a single point of failure, where the corrupted server can compromise the confidentiality and integrity of the audit log.

Decentralized Audit Log. Several works have proposed a decentralized audit log to address the single point of failure vulnerabilities. These schemes were designed for medical data [3, 13], supply chain [15, 16], and financial applications [34, 35]. Some schemes permit tamper resistance and access control to data objects being logged [36, 37]. However, these approaches do not hide the user identities (e.g., sender/receiver). Several works attempted to achieve either full anonymity [18] or partially anonymous [19]. There are several schemes that permit the validity of audit log to be verified publicly [17] or privately [18, 19]. Private validity verifiability requires every user in the system to participate and prove the integrity of their records during the audit phase.

IX Conclusion

We proposed 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates}, a privacy-preserving and immutable audit log scheme. 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} achieved immutability and resistance to single point of failure by leveraging blockchain, and achieved public verifiability of record validity using zero-knowledge proofs. We fully implemented 𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} and evaluated its performance by using Hyperledger Fabric and Amazon EC2.
